name: Zane Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do nights out of the supermarket distribution centre on the ring road, the big grey shed by the flyover. I clock on at ten, check the unit and the trailer, then run chilled and ambient stock out to six stores, back by six in the morning. I've been on the trunk runs eight years now, and I'm the one who takes new drivers out for their assessment. What I like is the empty motorway at three in the morning; what wears me out is the yard, waiting forty minutes for a loading bay because someone upstairs planned it badly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside the cab.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a flat over a bike shop with Dilan, my partner, who's a nurse on the stroke ward, so we're both night people. We've got about three months of money put by, which is fine as long as the car doesn't die. I'm also the union rep for the night drivers, which mostly means arguing about breaks and the camera they put in our cabs last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the drivers' room for two years: told you so. Every time head office gets excited about some new system, we end up with more screens and the same amount of work. Online I'd probably just share a joke about it and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job, which suits me. The thing that would still bother me is the monitoring, because a bit of AI is exactly what they'd use to score us on braking and break times. I don't need a computer telling me I took a corner hard when I've got a loaded double-deck trailer behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the trunk runs and keep the union stuff going, mainly pushing back on how the camera data gets used. I'd keep putting a bit away every month, about two hundred, because rent went up again in spring. Nothing dramatic, I'm not someone who changes things that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed, to be honest. It's the world I already know, with a few more gadgets I'll ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the monitoring bothers you. What happened with the camera last year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They fitted cameras facing the driver, and within a month a lad called Ryan got a warning for yawning at a red light. I took it to the depot manager with the union and we got it struck off his record. If AI is mostly hype, the only thing it'll really do at my depot is watch drivers yawn at red lights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dilan do with the next few years in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save for a deposit, slowly. Dilan wants a place with a garden, and on two normal wages that's maybe five years away. As long as the night rate holds, we're on track.

say: I'd tell the drivers' room I **told them so** about the hype.
I'd post a **joke** online and move on, because nothing really changes.
think: My **job stays mine**, and that suits me fine.
The real risk is AI used for **driver monitoring**, scoring every brake and break.
do: Keep running the **night trunk routes** to six stores as normal.
Push the union on **camera data** rules at the depot.
Put away about **two hundred** a month towards a deposit.
feel: **Relaxed**, because it's the world he already knows.
A little **irritated** at the gadgets he expects to ignore.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, the only thing it'll really do at my depot is watch drivers yawn at red lights.
fieldNote: His concern in a quiet world is **surveillance**, not job loss; the camera story clearly still angers him.
He speaks as a **union rep** first and a driver second.
Savings and a stable night rate make this feel **secure** to him.

steps.text: Keep running the night trunk routes from the ring road depot
Take the driver-camera rules to the depot manager with the union
Put two hundred a month into the deposit savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say keep your eyes open, because the office side is where it bites first. The planners and the transport desk would shrink, and that's people I know. I'd say it in the union meeting too: they come for the desk, then they come for the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, in the cab, not much changes for a few years, because nobody's putting a robot in a 44-tonne truck on the ring road next month. But the routing would all come from software, and software doesn't know the store in Hillcrest has a loading bay you can only reverse into from one side. My worry is they plan routes nobody can actually drive in the time given.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to put routing and timings into the agreement, so a human checks the plan before it hits us. I'd keep the savings going and maybe up it to three hundred, because if the office shrinks, overtime gets tighter. I'm not going to go and learn the new system unless they make me; that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled. My own wheel is safe for now, but I'd be watching good people on the desk get shown the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the desk would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, who's done the night planning for twenty years and knows every store manager by name. She's the reason my runs work at all. If software replaces Carol, the trucks keep moving, but nobody will pick up the phone when a trailer breaks down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the new system unless they make you. Is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I know some of the younger drivers would say I'm being stubborn. I've been driving trucks since I was nineteen and I've never needed a computer to tell me where Hillcrest is. I'll learn it when it's in my cab, not before.

say: I'd warn the union meeting that AI **comes for the desk** first, then the cab.
I'd tell drivers to **watch the office**, where colleagues will lose jobs first.
think: My own **driving** is safe for a few years in this world.
Software routes will set **impossible timings** for real loading bays.
do: Push for a **human check** on routes and timings in the union agreement.
Raise savings to about **three hundred** a month as overtime tightens.
Refuse to learn the **routing system** until it reaches his own cab.
feel: **Unsettled** for colleagues on the desk, though his own wheel feels safe.
**Defensive** about his experience being overruled by software.
S1.quote: I've been driving trucks since I was nineteen and I've never needed a computer to tell me where Hillcrest is.
fieldNote: He separates his own safety from his **colleagues' risk** clearly and sincerely.
His resistance to new tools is a point of **pride**, not ignorance.
He'd fight through **the union** rather than change himself.

steps.text: Get human checks on route timings written into the union agreement
Raise monthly savings from two hundred to three hundred
Keep driving trunk runs and skip the routing course until required

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loud: this needs stopping or slowing down, and the government needs to step in now. I'd be on every union call and I'd put it everywhere online. Motorway trunking is the easiest driving job there is to automate, and everyone in the industry knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is one of the first to go. What I do is depot to store on big straight roads at night, with no traffic. Even if robots take three years to load and unload, the driving part could be done by a self-driving truck with someone loading it at each end. I'd be thirty-two in 2031 with no other trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd throw myself into the union campaign for a slow rollout and a proper pay-off for drivers. I'd cut back hard, no holiday, and try to get to six months saved. I'd probably look at the forklift and warehouse side, because somebody still has to load the trailers until the robots come. I know that buys three years, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Two years is nothing. I'd lie awake doing the maths on the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dilan that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say her job is safer than mine, and that's a strange thing to admit. Nurses lift and comfort people, and nobody's building a robot that does that by 2031. I'd tell Dilan (my partner) that she might be carrying us both for a while, and I'd hate saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to her family in the summer, then the car, because I could cycle to the depot. We'd keep the flat as long as we could. I'd rather go without than move back in with my mum at thirty.

say: I'd demand the government **slow it down** and step in now.
I'd tell everyone that **motorway trunking** is the easiest driving to automate.
think: My job is among the **first to go** once self-driving trucks arrive.
At **thirty-two** in 2031 I'd have no other trade to fall back on.
do: Campaign through the union for a **slow rollout** and redundancy pay.
Cut spending hard to reach **six months** of savings.
Look at **warehouse loading** work to buy three more years.
feel: **Sick** and sleepless, doing the rent maths at night.
**Ashamed** that his partner might have to carry them both.
S2.quote: I'd tell Dilan (my partner) that she might be carrying us both for a while, and I'd hate saying it.
fieldNote: He sees **night motorway work** as the softest target and doesn't kid himself.
The **three-year gap** before robots only buys him warehouse work, in his view.
Pride and **gender roles** surface when he talks about Dilan supporting him.

steps.text: Join the union campaign for a slow rollout and driver pay-offs
Cancel the summer holiday and sell the car to save
Apply for forklift work loading trailers at the distribution centre
Lobby the local MP for a legal limit on driverless trucks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get rules in place before the trucks drive themselves, so let's use them. I'd push for a law that every self-driving truck has a qualified driver on board for the first years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years means I'm still driving until about 2034, if the robots come three years after the thinking AI. The office stuff goes in 2031, so the planning and the paperwork on my runs would be done by a machine by then. I'd have time to prepare, but I'm not good at preparing for things I hate the idea of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving, aiming for six months put by within two years. I'd do the union work properly, maybe go for a regional position. Dilan keeps telling me to look at an ambulance driving course, and maybe in this one I'd actually do it, around year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less sick than with two years. There's time to fight it, and fighting I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an ambulance course, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dilan sees the ambulance crews every shift and says they're always short of people who can drive under pressure. It's still driving, still people, and I can't see anyone letting a robot drive a cardiac patient. An ambulance is the one vehicle I can't picture anybody trusting a robot to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops you doing it sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money and the habit. Training means a pay drop for a year, and I like my runs. I'd keep putting it off until the robot trucks were on the road, which is probably too late.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get rules in place and should use them.
I'd push for a law requiring a **qualified driver** on board every self-driving truck.
think: I'd probably keep driving until around **2034**, with planning automated by 2031.
I know I'm **bad at preparing** for changes I dislike.
do: Build savings to **six months** within two years.
Stand for a **regional union** position to fight for driver rules.
Consider an **ambulance driving** course around year three.
feel: **Worried**, but less sick than with two years.
Stronger with a **fight** to put his energy into.
S3.quote: An ambulance is the one vehicle I can't picture anybody trusting a robot to drive.
fieldNote: Extra time turns his fear into **organising**, but not into retraining yet.
He admits **putting things off** until too late, which is honest.
The **ambulance** idea comes from his partner, not from himself.

steps.text: Build savings to six months of rent and bills within two years
Stand for the regional union committee for transport drivers
Price up an ambulance driving course for around 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse if they don't. I'd want retraining money for every driver paid by the companies that profit. Online I'd keep it simple: share the gains or don't do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like a career's worth of time. Robots for driving in 2039 means I'd be forty. I can drive until then and still have time for something else, if I do it right. The thinking side, the planning and the tachograph paperwork, would be gone by 2036, but I don't do much of that anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for now and save steadily. Around 2030 I'd do the ambulance course, or maybe a bus licence, because public transport might keep human drivers longer. The union fight would carry on the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easy, but manageable. Ten years is long enough that I'd stop thinking about it most weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, instead of putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first driverless trial truck on our ring road. That's when it becomes real for me. Until then it's just talk in the papers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the young drivers you assess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a second licence early, bus or ambulance, while they're young and the training's cheap. The new lads I take out for assessments should get a second licence before they get comfortable, because comfortable is what got me.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for an unfair rollout.
I'd demand **retraining money** paid by the firms that profit from automation.
think: Robots in 2039 means I'd be **forty**, with time for something else.
Losing the **paperwork side** in 2036 barely touches my day.
do: Keep driving trunk runs and **save steadily** for now.
Take an **ambulance or bus** licence around 2030.
Carry on the **union fight** for a fair transition.
feel: **Manageable**, with long stretches of not thinking about it.
Still a low **worry** about leaving it too late.
S4.quote: The new lads I take out for assessments should get a second licence before they get comfortable, because comfortable is what got me.
fieldNote: He needs a **visible trigger**, like a trial truck, before he'll act.
His advice to young drivers shows **regret** about his own habits.
Even with ten years, he expects his **income to change** before he's forty.

steps.text: Keep driving the trunk runs and save a fixed sum monthly
Take a bus or ambulance licence around 2030
Campaign for company-funded retraining money for drivers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. My runs are the easy kind to automate and I'd have nothing lined up. What would help is a proper deal: redundancy pay based on years served and a paid retraining place, so I'm not choosing between rent and a course. Give me a year's wage and a training place and I'll go quietly; give me a robot and a leaflet and I'll be on the picket line.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people loading the trucks at the stores at five in the morning. Everyone talks about drivers, but the lads on the night shift at the store doors are just as easy to replace. I'd want them in the deal too.

headlineQuote: Give me a year's wage and a training place and I'll go quietly; give me a robot and a leaflet and I'll be on the picket line.
portrait: A **27-year-old** night trunk driver and union rep who assesses new drivers at a supermarket depot.
He rents a flat with his **nurse partner** Dilan and saves for a deposit.
He sees monitoring as the threat in a quiet world and **job loss** in the fast AGI ones.
He fights through the **union** rather than retraining, and admits he puts change off.
With ten years he'd take a **second licence**, ambulance or bus, around 2030.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because night motorway trunking is easy to automate and he'd have nothing lined up.
whatWouldHelp: **Redundancy pay** based on years served plus a paid retraining place.
A deal that also covers the **store loaders** on the night shift.
